summary: A 1976 paper describing a distributed capability computing system, where access to resources is controlled by unforgeable tokens called capabilities. It was prepared for a conference and is shared as a preprint.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 712 describes a distributed computing system that lets a process use capabilities supported by another host. The local and remote systems pass requests and results through network messages while retaining capability-based access controls.

questions: what is a capability computing system
how does the dccs invoke a remote capability
how does rfc 712 control remote capability access
subtitle: A preprint describing remote capability access across different computer systems.

tldr.problem: A distributed system needs to let a process use a resource on another computer while preserving the local system's access controls.
tldr.mechanism: The DCCS represents remote capabilities with requestors and descriptors, forwards invocation parameters to the supporting host, and returns results to the requesting process.
tldr.outcome: The paper describes an experimental protocol and applications including shared information and network resource management. It notes that recovery and other issues are outside its scope.

today: RFC 712 identifies itself as a preprint prepared for submission to a conference. It says the DCCS mechanisms were being implemented experimentally and lists several operational issues outside the paper's scope.

sections.title: Capabilities in the Local System
sections.content:
The paper introduces an idealized Capability Computing System (CCS). Each process has a protected capability list containing references to objects it may access, and it invokes a capability to request an operation.

An invocation can pass both data and other capabilities. A service routine can be in another process or computer, while the invoking process remains isolated except for the parameters exchanged.
sections.plainLanguage: A process holds protected references to the objects it may use. It asks an object to perform an operation by invoking its capability.

sections.title: Emulating a Remote Capability
sections.content:
The DCCS lets one host emulate a capability that is supported on another host. When a process invokes the local requestor, its host sends the parameters and a descriptor identifying the remote host and capability to the supporting host.

The supporting host invokes the real capability and sends the result back. If the result includes a capability, the supporting host allocates a slot and returns a descriptor that the emulating host turns into another requestor.
sections.plainLanguage: A local computer can pass a request to the computer that supports the capability, then return the result to its process. A returned capability can also be represented locally by a new requestor.

sections.title: Access, Timing, and Limitations
sections.content:
The paper says the mechanism needs authorization checks so one host cannot invoke capabilities on another host without permission. It describes a bit vector at the supporting host to record which hosts may access a capability, and a message to authorize passing a capability onward.

Long-running invocations are kept as pending requests so a host can continue handling other work. The paper explicitly leaves issues such as errors, restart recovery, network failures, message-size limits, and resource problems outside its discussion.
sections.plainLanguage: Hosts must check which remote systems may use each capability. Because an operation may take a long time, requests can remain pending while other work continues.
